final_answer:
SHORT ANSWER. (1) The husband's best route is a motion to reopen filed with the immigration court to rescind the August 1, 2025 in absentia order for lack of notice under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii), and 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii). That ground has no deadline, so it is timely on April 1, 2026, and no filing fee is charged for it. (2) Separately, the USCIS denials can be attacked by a USCIS motion to reopen/reconsider, but the regular deadline has long passed, so that route is weak. The more practical fix is to restore his eligibility to adjust in court and have the I-130 re-adjudicated.

A. IMMIGRATION COURT. 1. Vehicle: a motion to reopen and rescind the in absentia order. The statute allows rescission at any time if the alien shows he did not receive notice under INA 239(a)(1) or (2) (or was in custody through no fault of his own). A motion on the 'exceptional circumstances' ground, INA 240(b)(5)(C)(i), must be filed within 180 days. That period ran from August 1, 2025 to about January 28, 2026, so it is expired and is not the right ground. 2. Content: file with the immigration court that entered the order, on the court's e-filing system (ECAS) or on paper, with a cover page. It needs (a) a sworn declaration from the husband stating that the address used was never provided by him, that he never received the NTA or hearing notice, and that he believed his case was pending with USCIS; (b) proof of the address he actually gave USCIS (the I-130/I-485 filing receipts and the I-797 notices), plus evidence the RFE and NTA were mailed to a different address (envelopes, USCIS records, FOIA material); (c) a statement that he is not seeking reopening on exceptional-circumstances grounds; and (d) a copy of the order. The motion should say that relief is available upon reopening, specifically adjustment of status as the spouse of a U.S. citizen, and attach a prima facie showing, though a lack-of-notice motion does not require relief to be shown. Include the I-130 and I-485 materials as an offer of proof, and a proposed order. Serve DHS/ICE OPLA. 3. Automatic stay: under 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii), filing a timely lack-of-notice motion automatically stays removal until the IJ rules. Counsel should be aware that he is currently removable, and ICE may arrest him, before filing. 4. Notice law: the NTA must be sent to the address the alien provided, and a hearing notice sent to a wrong address is not proper notice. Beware of Campos-Chaves v. Garland, 602 U.S. 447 (2024): a defective NTA (for example, one omitting time or place) can be cured by a later hearing notice, but the alien must actually have been properly served with that notice. Because the husband never received anything, he can argue that the statutory notice requirements were not met. The burden is on him, and DHS may argue that he had a duty to update his address (INA 239(a)(1)(F), (a)(2)(B)). The government is entitled to rely on the last address provided, so the address evidence is critical. 5. Fees: no fee for a motion to reopen in absentia under 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) (8 CFR 1003.24(b)(2)(iii)); this was reported as unchanged by the July 2025 H.R. 1 fee increases (EOIR PM 25-36). Had the motion been brought under 240(b)(5)(C)(i), the fee would apply, reportedly $900 under H.R. 1 and not waivable; I could not open EOIR's memo to verify the amounts. If the motion is granted, new proceedings resume. The fee to file the I-485 with the court (or lodge it) must be handled according to the IJ's instructions: a pending I-485 filing fee was already paid to USCIS, and EOIR's additional fees under H.R. 1 may apply to other applications (for example, a new I-485 filed with the court or a cancellation application). Check the current EOIR fee schedule before filing.

B. USCIS. 1. The I-130 denial was for failure to respond to the RFE, which USCIS treats as abandonment or failure to establish eligibility. A denial for abandonment cannot be appealed (8 CFR 103.2(b)(15)) but can be challenged by a motion to reopen under 8 CFR 103.5(a)(2) (Form I-290B). The motion must be filed within 30 days (33 days by mail), measured from the decision; late filing is excused only if the delay was reasonable and beyond the applicant's control, and that exception applies to motions to reopen, not reconsider. Here the denial dates (December 5, 2023 and January 15, 2024) are more than two years old, and the couple was never told. A motion could still argue that the failure was due to USCIS's own error in mailing and that the delay was reasonable, but approval is discretionary. USCIS may also reopen on its own motion (8 CFR 103.5(a)(5)(i)); a request to the service center citing agency error is worth making. I-290B fee is about $800 (verify). 2. A denied I-485 itself cannot be appealed (8 CFR 103.2(b)(15)/1245.2(a)(5)(ii)), but renewed adjustment can be sought before the IJ. If USCIS does not reopen, the practical remedy is: after the order is rescinded, the husband files a new I-130 with USCIS (current fee for paper filing about $675; verify) and asks the IJ to continue the case while it is adjudicated; the IJ lacks jurisdiction over the I-130 but may continue under 8 CFR 1003.29 for good cause (Matter of L-A-B-R-, 27 I&N Dec. 405 (A.G. 2018)). Once the I-130 is approved the IJ can adjudicate his I-485 (8 CFR 1245.2(a)(1)), with a new I-485 and a fee. Eligibility should survive: he entered with inspection and admission on a B-2, and as an immediate relative of a U.S. citizen his overstay does not bar adjustment (INA 245(a), 245(c)); a visa is immediately available. A possible issue is whether B-2 admission with preconceived intent to marry and stay is a misrepresentation (INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i); 9 FAM 302.9-4(B)(3), the '90-day rule', not binding, but marrying 19 days after entry would trigger it): the couple should be prepared to rebut an inference of willful misrepresentation. Also note that failure to appear may have consequences for relief that depend on voluntary departure; an old in absentia order, once rescinded, no longer applies.

C. If the motion to reopen is denied, he can appeal to the BIA within 30 days (8 CFR 1003.38) and petition for review in the court of appeals within 30 days of the BIA's decision (INA 242(b)(1)). The IJ's sua sponte authority (8 CFR 1003.23(b)(1)) is a fallback. Also consider a bar on removal if DHS acts before the ruling, and a motion to stay removal (EOIR-... only for non-automatic cases). RECOMMENDATION: file the lack-of-notice motion immediately, gather address evidence, request the court record (ROP) and USCIS file (FOIA), and consult counsel. This is general information, not legal advice. Caveat: I could not fetch the primary text of the statute, regulations, or EOIR memo (blocked), so some details are from secondary sources and memory.
